analysis.one_liner: Requires drugmakers to share FDA filings with the patent office, exposing drug patents built on inconsistent claims.
analysis.headline: The Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee reported the bill favorably to the full Senate on July 28, 2026; it now sits on the Senate calendar with no floor vote yet, while Congress remains in session.
analysis.plain_summary: Drug companies currently talk to two agencies: the FDA, which decides whether a drug is safe and effective, and the Patent Office, which decides how long the company can block cheaper copies. Companies sometimes describe the same data differently to each office — favorably to the FDA to win approval, and favorably to the Patent Office to win broad patents. This bill requires companies to hand the Patent Office the information they give the FDA and to certify the two records match. If a company got or kept a patent by withholding required information, cheaper generic or biosimilar makers accused of infringement could raise that failure as a legal defense, shortening the monopoly and speeding up lower-priced competition.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and payers who buy brand-name prescription drugs, because weaker or shorter patents mean generic and biosimilar copies can reach the market sooner and prices fall. Generic and biosimilar manufacturers also gain a new legal defense in patent lawsuits brought by brand-name companies.

how_it_helps.text: Drug sponsors and patent holders must certify to the FDA that the information they submit is consistent with what they told the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office, and must submit to the Patent Office any information material to patentability that they give the FDA, including statements and characterizations of analytical data from a drug application.

The bill creates a new legal defense for a person accused of infringing a drug patent if the patent owner or a previous owner negligently or intentionally failed to disclose the required information to the Patent Office.
Failing to submit the required certification becomes a prohibited act that the FDA can enforce, alongside other prohibitions on what drug applicants may do.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug makers and biotech companies, whose patents become harder to obtain and easier to invalidate when their FDA and Patent Office records must match, shortening the years of monopoly pricing on their most profitable products. They also bear compliance costs of dual filings and certifications.

drawbacks.text: The requirements apply mainly going forward — to new applications and patents issued after enactment — so patents already granted before the bill becomes law are only covered for new filings and communications, limiting the effect on existing drug monopolies.
The certifications are made only 'to the best knowledge' of the sponsor or holder, a knowledge standard that makes the duty harder to enforce than an absolute guarantee of accuracy.

Enforcement works through lawsuits: a generic or biosimilar maker has to be sued for infringement and raise the defense in court, so relief is slow, uneven, and unavailable to a 'covered foreign person' under the committee-reported version — which excludes many foreign generic manufacturers from using it.

Information shared with the Patent Office keeps trade-secret and confidential protections as if held by the FDA, which limits public visibility into exactly what companies disclosed — though the Patent Office may override those protections where the public needs the information to understand the scope of a patent claim.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This is a narrow, targeted integrity fix rather than a direct price cap, so its effect on drug prices is indirect and will build slowly as new patents are issued under the rule. Against that, it addresses a real gap — companies quietly describing the same data two different ways to two agencies — without publicly exposing trade secrets, and the committee version even adds protections for foreign rivals. The main honest criticism is that it mostly reaches future patents and leans on litigation, so patients may wait years before seeing any difference at the pharmacy.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Health Committee reported the bill favorably with an amendment on July 28, 2026, and it now sits on the Senate's legislative calendar waiting for floor time and a vote; Congress is still in session, so nothing is final.

narrative.text: Senator Hassan introduced the bill on August 1, 2025 with Senator Hawley, making it a bipartisan pairing from the start, and it was referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee.
The committee held a hearing on March 19, 2026, then ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute on June 17, 2026, and formally reported it on July 28, 2026.

The reported substitute keeps the core disclosure and enforcement structure but adds a condition: the new infringement defense is not available to a 'covered foreign person' as defined in the Defense Production Act.
The bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 528, the step just before floor consideration, and no Senate vote has occurred.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far no one has lost ground: brand-name drug makers keep operating under existing patents without the new disclosure duties, while the bill's backers have moved it further along the Senate pipeline than most bills ever get. If it stalls on the calendar, the companies that benefit are the ones whose patents were never exposed to matching scrutiny.

for.name: Sen. Margaret Wood Hassan
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate on August 1, 2025.

for.name: Sen. Josh Hawley
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction — Hassan introduced it 'for herself and Mr. Hawley' — making it bipartisan from day one.

for.name: Sen. Bill Cassidy
for.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
for.what_they_did: Managed the committee's markup and formally reported the bill favorably to the Senate with an amendment in the nature of a substitute on July 28, 2026.

sides.party_line_note: A Democrat sponsored the bill with one Republican cosponsor, and the Republican-chaired HELP Committee reported it favorably with an amendment; no opposition has appeared in the record yet.

industries.note: Their patents become harder to win and easier to defeat when they must give the Patent Office the same data and statements they give the FDA, and infringers can raise non-disclosure as a defense. For patients that means monopolies can end sooner and generic competition can start earlier, so the industry's interest here runs against cheaper medicine.

They get a new legal defense in patent infringement suits when a brand-name patent owner failed to disclose required information, making it easier to launch lower-priced copies. The committee version, however, bars covered foreign persons from using the defense, narrowing who benefits.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has cleared committee and sits on the Senate calendar, which is further than most bills get, but Senate floor time is scarce and most calendar bills never reach a vote unless leadership prioritizes them or they ride on a larger health package. With bipartisan sponsorship and a favorable committee report, it could be folded into a broader drug-pricing or FDA user-fee bill; otherwise it may sit on the calendar through the end of the Congress without a vote.
